title: Why We Argue
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing days before a U.S. presidential election, Stuart argues that Americans' poor collective argumentation skills make the case for sustained argumentative work in secondary classrooms. He distinguishes between arguing often, which Americans do plenty of, and arguing well, in the "earnest and amicable" way he says the country needs. His practical answer is to increase the sheer quantity of structured argumentative practice -- through frequent Pop-Up Debates and close analysis of how others argue (claims, evidence, reasoning, counterclaims) -- because mini-sermonizing a skill's value is hollow if students aren't actually doing much of it. He then lists specific mini-sermon talking points he uses across the year to help students value getting better at arguing, from the PVLEGS delivery framework to the idea that disagreement is a sign of respect. Stuart frames all of this as apologetics work he genuinely enjoys, arguing that his own enjoyment while mini-sermonizing is part of what makes the message land as winsome and sure.
points: Stuart's diagnosis of the 2024 election moment -- "we argue, but we do not argue well" -- becomes the motivating case for sustained Pop-Up Debate practice in his classroom.

His rule of thumb is that mini-sermonizing a skill is "silly" unless students are actually spending real class time doing it, which is why quantity (nine PUDs in AP courses, six on-level, by the time of writing) comes before persuasion.
He teaches students to examine how others argue by identifying claims, evidence, reasoning, and counterclaims in real texts -- a second, complementary path to better arguing.

One especially sticky mini-sermon point: "when someone disagrees with an argument you've made, that's a beautiful sign of respect" -- reframing pushback as evidence of being taken seriously rather than an attack.
quotes: Do we argue in this country? Boy, do we. But do we argue well in this country? No. We do not.
It's silly to mini-sermonize anything that you're not doing a lot in your classes. In other words, Value proof for a type of work is often in the pudding.
When someone disagrees with an argument you've made, that's a beautiful sign of respect. It means they listened to you and took your argument seriously.
Great arguments typically do a few basic things: paraphrase someone else's argument, then either A) agree with it while adding on, B) disagree with it with reasons, or C) complicate it.
How you deliver an argument is half the battle. It's possible for folks to make a terrible argument but sound amazing, and it's possible for folks to make stellar arguments but sound so bad.
They are fun. I make it a point to enjoy myself when I'm talking about the importance of getting better at arguing. As I seek to enjoy myself, I tap in to being winsome and sure.
